final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

comments.body:
Done — report attached. Stayed inside the three things you asked for.

**Short version:**

**1. Trainer or DIY?** Both, but the cheap version of hiring. You've actually got two problems and they don't have the same answer — pulling is mechanical and very DIY-able, reactivity is emotional and punishes mistakes (working too close makes it worse, not just slower). So: do the daily walking work yourself, and buy structured expert eyes on the reactivity piece for $300. Your case is a favourable one — 14 months, no bite history, border collie brain — so paying $2,400 up front isn't warranted yet.

**2. Three options with real prices:**
- **HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 — $300**, six weeks, online, built specifically for leash reactivity. Next cohort **Wed Aug 19 at 6:15pm**, which fits your evenings. Possibly cheaper: they give adopters a discount and it extends to other coalition shelters, so ask.
- **Stacy's Wag'N'Train — $190** one-hour behaviour consult (credited free into a package), or **$400/month** for weekly private sessions. CPDT-KA, San Jose, does dog-dog reactivity. Best-value 1:1.
- **D For Dogz — $2,400** for six weeks of private coaching on your own walking routes. Premium option, highest touch.

Zoom Room fits on method and geography but won't publish prices, so it's a backup. SIRIUS is $249 but its adolescent class isn't reactivity work — wrong tool.

**3. Four-week plan** is in the tree as Week 0 through Week 4 subtasks, one per week, each with the specific drills, doses and an end-of-week check. Week 0 is the errand + baseline, week 1 is management and mechanics with no other dogs, week 2 adds Engage-Disengage Level 1, week 3 goes to Level 2 and closes distance, week 4 combines them and has an explicit go/escalate decision.

**Two things worth flagging:**
- The single most useful number you'll produce is in Week 0: the distance at which he can still eat a treat *and* still turn back to you. Everything in weeks 2–4 happens at or beyond it. Without it the protocols don't have a starting point.
- HSSV doesn't do private training for the public, only classes — so if you want 1:1, it has to be Stacy or D For Dogz. That's why option 2 exists.

**Your next moves** (all in the tree with contact details): email DogTraining@hssv.org about the adopter discount, register for the Aug 19 cohort before it fills, and buy the front-clip harness this weekend.

Setting to needs_review. Parent is left open rather than done because the enrolment and the kit purchase are yours to make.

One note: the original "Write the week-by-week plan" stub is superseded — that deliverable now lives in the five Week 0–4 subtasks, which are more useful than a single task would have been. Safe to close it.

report.markdown:
A 14-month rescue border collie mix who pulls and barks at dogs is close to the textbook case for this kind of work: adolescent, no bite history, highly trainable breed. All three answers below assume force-free methods only.

---

## 1. Trainer or DIY?

**Do both — but buy the cheap version of "hire."** Enrol in HSSV's reactive-dog class ($300, six weeks, evenings, online) and do the daily walking work yourself using the plan in section 3. Only escalate to a private in-home trainer if there's no movement by the end of week 4.

The reason is that you actually have two different problems, and they don't have the same answer.

| | Leash pulling | Barking at dogs |
|---|---|---|
| Nature of problem | Mechanical / trained habit | Emotional — a stress response |
| DIY-able? | Yes, readily | Risky without coaching |
| What can go wrong | Slow progress | Working too close makes it *worse* |

Pulling is a mechanics problem and good instructions genuinely solve it. Reactivity is different: <cite index="60-1">stress responses divide into fight (barking, lunging), flight, freeze, or "fool around" behaviours</cite>, and <cite index="60-2,60-3">the barking dog is typically hurling himself toward the trigger out of fear, anxiety or frustration, having real difficulty disengaging</cite>. That's not disobedience, so it doesn't respond to being told off.

**Why not pure DIY.** The load-bearing skill is reading distance and stress, and it's the hardest thing to self-teach from text. <cite index="60-8">Every time your dog practises an undesired reaction outside training time, he goes backward and continues to feel stressed around the trigger</cite> — so mistakes actively cost you ground. <cite index="46-5">Owners often need professional coaching to develop the timing, reading skills and confidence that reactive-dog training requires</cite>. Six weeks of structured instruction for $300 is cheap insurance against months of accidental backsliding.

**Why not a full private trainer immediately.** The case is favourable. <cite index="4-1">Reactivity is a highly modifiable behaviour, and through prevention, training and practice even very "explosive" dogs can learn calmer responses around other dogs</cite>. Crucially, no bite history: <cite index="45-1">many owners do succeed with these techniques, especially for mild to moderate reactivity — professional help is the call if the dog has bitten or attempted to bite, if reactivity is escalating, or if you feel overwhelmed</cite>. And the cost gap is wide: $300 versus $2,400 for six weeks of private coaching.

**Escalate to a private trainer or a veterinary behaviourist immediately if:**
- Any bite or attempted bite on a dog or person. This also disqualifies him from every group class listed below.
- Reactivity is escalating rather than plateauing.
- You cannot find *any* distance where he'll take a treat with a dog in sight.
- Reactivity to people too, or barking at windows indoors.
- You're dreading or avoiding walks. That's reason enough on its own.

**One hard rule on method.** Positive-reinforcement providers only. Aversive tools suppress the bark while leaving the fear intact. This ruled out at least one prominent local outfit selling an $800 four-week private package.

---

## 2. Three local options, with real prices

### Recommended: HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1 (Reactive Dogs)" — $300
Humane Society Silicon Valley, Milpitas · DogTraining@hssv.org

<cite index="52-13,52-14">Designed specifically for dogs struggling with reactivity — online via Zoom, dogs 8 months and older, no prior bite history on dogs or people</cite>. <cite index="52-15">It covers science-based positive-reinforcement strategies including threshold work, impulse control, calm exits and real-life coping skills</cite>. <cite index="52-17">Six-week course, one session per week: the first is 90 minutes, then five sessions of 50 minutes</cite>, <cite index="52-18">for dogs who bark, lunge or worry but have not caused injury</cite>.

- **Next cohort: Wed 19 Aug 2026, 6:15pm** — an evening slot. Register: `pro.gofundme.com/event/e826622`
- <cite index="52-20">$300 general registration</cite>
- **Ask about the adopter discount.** <cite index="10-5">Adopters receive a discount; email DogTraining@hssv.org to find out if you qualify</cite>, and <cite index="10-7">it applies to pets adopted within the past year from HSSV or any weC.A.R.E. Community Coalition adoption centre</cite>. Worth asking even if you adopted elsewhere.
- **Then Level 2, $300** — <cite index="52-24">an in-person class where you and your reactive dog work in a controlled group setting with real-time coaching, one 50-minute session a week for six weeks</cite>. This is the graduation exercise you can't manufacture on your own.
- **Caveat:** <cite index="10-6">HSSV does not currently offer private training or consultation to the general public</cite> — referrals only. So it can't be your 1:1.

### Best-value 1:1: Stacy's Wag'N'Train — $190 consult / $400 a month
Stacy Braslau-Schneck, CPDT-KA · Willow Glen / San Jose · Stacy@wagntrain.com

<cite index="21-4">A former dolphin trainer using humane, positive methods that account for the dog's emotional needs as well as the owner's, with programmes starting from a consultation to establish goals and issues</cite>. <cite index="19-3">CPDT-KA certified, APDT and Pet Professional Guild member, 20+ years' experience</cite>, and <cite index="9-4">working specifically on leash reactivity and aggression toward people and other dogs</cite>.

| Option | Price |
|---|---|
| Behaviour consultation / evaluation (~1 hr) | <cite index="35-0">$190, or included in any package</cite> |
| Package 1 — weekly 1-hour sessions | <cite index="35-2">$400/month, or $1,000 for 3 months (12 sessions, saves $200)</cite> |
| Package 2 — fortnightly, 6 months (12 sessions) | <cite index="35-3">$1,000, or $200/month</cite> |
| Package 3 — monthly, 6 months (6 sessions) | <cite index="35-4">$500, or $100/month</cite> |
| Follow-up single sessions after a package | <cite index="35-5">$130 each</cite> |

<cite index="37-1,37-2">In-person across central Silicon Valley / Santa Clara County and virtually; serving Willow Glen, San Jose and mid-Santa Clara County since 1998</cite>. **Open question:** evening/weekend slots aren't published — ask.

### Premium: D For Dogz — $2,400 / six weeks
Kaajal · Silicon Valley / Palo Alto

A dedicated leash-reactive programme run on your own turf: <cite index="55-6">sessions take place in your home, your neighbourhood and your regular walking routes — where your dog actually encounters other dogs, people and moving objects</cite>.

- **Private Coaching — <cite index="55-14">$2,400 / 6 weeks</cite>:** <cite index="55-15">for owners who want to learn to train the dog themselves, with every session building handler skill and confidence</cite>, plus weekly real-world neighbourhood walks and priority trainer access between sessions by call, text or email.
- **Day Training — <cite index="55-9">$4,200 / 6 weeks</cite>:** includes a 90-minute goal-setting session; the trainer works your dog in your home and neighbourhood twice a week and you join every third session.
- <cite index="55-3">Enrolling in the full programme saves $420.</cite>

### Considered and set aside
- **Zoom Room Santa Clara** — force-free and explicit about it (<cite index="12-3,12-4">every programme built on positive reinforcement; no prong collars, no shock collars, no dominance-based methods</cite>), right geography, free 30-min orientation. But publishes **no prices** — "contact the store." Backup only.
- **SIRIUS Puppy & Dog Training** — <cite index="15-2">$249 for five weekly 50-minute sessions</cite>, many South Bay locations, but Dog Training I is a general adolescent class, not reactivity work. Wrong tool.

**Sanity-check any quote against the local market:** private in-home training in San Jose runs about $100–$175 a session, with behaviour-modification work $125–$250 and structured programmes $500–$1,200+. Sunnyvale and Mountain View skew higher.

---

## 3. The first four weeks

Two skills, taught separately, then combined. Full detail lives in the Week 0–4 subtasks; this is the shape.

**Week 0 (this weekend) — kit and baseline.** Buy a front-clip harness — <cite index="26-1">front-clipping harnesses cause your dog to turn and look back at you, encouraging check-ins and discouraging pulling</cite>. Add a 6 ft leash, a 15–30 ft long line, a clicker, and two tiers of treats: ordinary kibble for leash work, and high-value food used *only* for dog-sightings. Then record your baseline: at what distance does he notice a dog, and at what distance does he bark? **The distance where he can still eat and still turn back to you is your working distance** — everything else happens at or beyond it.

**Week 1 — management and mechanics, no other dogs.** <cite index="60-7">Before starting a training plan, use management to reduce how often your dog is reacting at all</cite>. Reroute to the quietest streets and times. Drill the emergency U-turn until it's automatic — <cite index="60-12">lure him around with a treat at his nose, or toss "find-it" treats on the ground as you change direction together</cite> — and rehearse it with no dog present so it works when one appears. Then 2 × 5 min of loose-leash work daily, in the driveway or garden only. <cite index="26-3">The secret is simple: don't move in the direction your dog is pulling.</cite> Leash goes tight, you stop dead; slack returns, you move off. He's a border collie mix at 14 months, so add 10–15 min of daily nose work or puzzle feeding — lowering baseline arousal makes everything else easier.

**Week 2 — Engage-Disengage Level 1.** Change how he *feels* before asking him to behave differently. <cite index="30-2">Level 1 rewards the dog for engaging with the trigger while not showing a stress response, which builds positive feelings toward it.</cite> The steps: <cite index="60-13,60-14,60-15">start at a distance where he isn't reacting and stay quiet so he notices the dog himself; click the moment he looks at it; feed when he turns back to you — and if he reacts or doesn't turn back, move further away and reset at an easier distance</cite>. <cite index="60-16">Aim for 3–5 successful reps in a row at the same distance before progressing.</cite> Practise where *you* control the distance — a bench 100 ft from a park entrance, a car park near a dog-walking route — not on random walks. Three or four sessions of 5–10 minutes, and stop early. <cite index="60-12">Take a break at even subtle stress signals: excessive lip-licking, yawning, or scratching.</cite>

**Week 3 — Level 2, then close the gap.** <cite index="30-3">Level 2 rewards the alternative behaviour of turning away from the trigger — a behaviour incompatible with barking at or lunging toward it.</cite> <cite index="60-18,60-19,60-20">Let him notice the dog, wait 1–5 seconds to see if he looks away on his own, click the instant he disengages, then feed; if he fixates for more than 5 seconds, go back to Level 1.</cite> Before closing distance at all, <cite index="60-17">keep playing Level 1 until he's calmly engaged with the trigger from every direction</cite> — a dog jogging past at 60 ft is much harder than one standing still. Shrink distance by a few feet, never half the gap.

**Week 4 — combine, then decide.** Run a normal evening walk with both skills as one fluent sequence: he looks, he looks back, he gets paid, you continue or U-turn. <cite index="7-3">There's no pressure for him to get close to another dog</cite> — <cite index="7-2">if the goal is passing dogs on the other side of the street without barking, you don't need to push closer</cite>. Start thinning treats for loose-leash walking only; keep paying every dog-sighting. Then compare against your week 0 notes: has the barking distance shrunk, is he recovering faster, is he checking in unprompted?

- **Any improvement → keep going.** Same structure for weeks 5–8, then HSSV Top Dogs Level 2 for in-person work around other reactive dogs.
- **No movement, or worse → book Stacy's $190 consultation.** Bring your baseline notes and this plan.

---

## What to do today

1. **Email DogTraining@hssv.org** about the adopter discount — you're a rescue adopter, this may be materially cheaper.
2. **Register for Top Dogs Level 1** before the 19 Aug cohort fills. Reactivity classes are capped.
3. **Buy the front-clip harness and two tiers of treats** this weekend, and write down the baseline.
4. Optionally, **email Stacy@wagntrain.com** to ask about evening slots, so the 1:1 fallback is warm.

subtasks.title: Decide: DIY vs. hire a trainer for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
Question 1 of the brief — DIY vs. hire.

RECOMMENDATION: Hybrid, weighted toward hiring — but a cheap version of hiring. Do the daily work yourself, and buy structured expert eyes on the reactivity piece specifically. Concretely: enrol in HSSV's Top Dogs Level 1 ($300, evenings, online) and self-manage the loose-leash work using the week-by-week plan. Only escalate to a private in-home trainer ($400–$2,400) if you see no movement by end of week 4.

WHY NOT PURE DIY:
- The two problems are not equally DIY-able. Leash pulling is a mechanical/training problem and is very learnable from good instructions. Reactivity is an EMOTIONAL problem — the barking is a stress response, not disobedience — and it needs desensitisation and counter-conditioning done at the right distance, with correct timing. Getting the distance or timing wrong makes it worse, because every unmanaged reaction is rehearsal that sets training back.
- The load-bearing skill is reading subtle stress signals (lip-licking, yawning, scratching, fixating >5 seconds) and knowing when to bail. That is the single hardest thing to self-teach from text, and it's exactly what a coach corrects in real time.
- Owner timing and confidence is itself a common failure point; professional coaching exists as much to train the handler as the dog.

WHY NOT FULL PRIVATE TRAINER IMMEDIATELY:
- This is a favourable case. 14 months = adolescent, i.e. normal peak age for reactivity to show up, and highly modifiable. Border collie mixes are exceptionally trainable and reinforcement-driven.
- No bite history mentioned — barking and pulling only. That keeps it in "mild to moderate" territory, where owners frequently do succeed with good protocols, and it also keeps every local programme open (all of them screen out bite history).
- Owner has evenings and weekends — enough for the 5–10 min daily reps the protocols actually need. Frequency matters far more than session length.
- Cost gap is large: $300 for a six-week reactivity course vs. $2,400 for six weeks of private coaching. Start cheap.

ESCALATE TO A PRIVATE TRAINER (or a veterinary behaviourist) IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR:
- Any bite, or attempt to bite, a dog or a person — stop DIY, go straight to a professional. This also disqualifies the dog from the group classes.
- Reactivity escalating rather than plateauing over 4 weeks.
- You cannot find a distance at which the dog will take a treat and disengage — meaning you can't get "under threshold" anywhere on your normal routes.
- Reactivity to people as well as dogs, or barking/lunging inside the home at windows.
- You feel overwhelmed or are avoiding walks. That's a legitimate reason to hire on its own.

NON-NEGOTIABLE ON METHOD: use force-free / positive-reinforcement providers only. Aversive tools (prong, shock/e-collar) suppress the bark while leaving the underlying fear intact, and can worsen dog-dog reactivity. This ruled out at least one high-visibility local outfit that sells a $800 4-week private package.

subtasks.description: Question 3 of the brief. Build a concrete 4-week plan the owner can execute on evenings and weekends. Must cover both problems: loose-leash walking and dog reactivity. Each week needs specific daily/weekly actions with time commitments, not general advice. Ground it in established protocols (engage-disengage, BAT/LAT, pattern games, pressure-free equipment).

subtasks.title: Week 0 (this weekend): buy kit and set the baseline
subtasks.description:
Do this BEFORE week 1 starts. One errand + 20 minutes of note-taking.

BUY:
- Front-clip / no-pull harness (Easy Walk style). This is the single highest-leverage purchase. The front clip turns the dog toward you when he forges ahead, which kills leverage and encourages check-ins. Do NOT use a prong or shock collar — they suppress the bark while leaving the fear intact and can make dog-dog reactivity worse.
- 6 ft fixed-length leash for training walks, plus a 15–30 ft long line for sniffing/decompression in open space. No retractable leads.
- A clicker.
- Two tiers of treats: ordinary kibble for loose-leash work, and HIGH-value (cheese, chicken, hot dog, freeze-dried liver) reserved exclusively for dog-sightings. The high-value stuff must not appear at any other time.
- A treat pouch you can get into one-handed.

BASELINE NOTES (write these down, you will want them in week 4):
- At what distance does he first notice another dog? At what distance does he start barking? Guess in car-lengths.
- Which streets/times are worst? Which are quietest?
- Will he take a treat when a dog is visible at 30 ft? At 60 ft? The distance where he can still eat and still turn back to you is your working distance — everything in weeks 1-4 happens at or beyond it.
- How long does he fixate before exploding?

DOWNLOAD (free): HSSV Reactive Dog Training Guide — https://www.hssv.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Reactive-Dog-Training-Guide-7.11.25.pdf

subtasks.title: Week 1: management + loose-leash foundations in zero-distraction settings
subtasks.description:
GOAL FOR THE WEEK: stop the rehearsal, and build the mechanics somewhere boring. You are NOT working on other dogs this week. Every unmanaged explosion is practice at exploding, so week 1 is about reducing the number of reactions to near zero while you build the tools.

MANAGEMENT (all week, non-negotiable):
- Reroute walks to the quietest streets and least busy times you identified in week 0. Industrial streets, cul-de-sacs, school grounds after hours, big empty car parks in the evening.
- Practise the EMERGENCY U-TURN until it's automatic. Lure him around by putting a treat at his nose, or toss a handful of treats on the ground and change direction as you both move toward them. Rehearse it 10 times a day with no dog present so it works when one appears.
- If a dog appears at close range and you have no room: U-turn and leave. Do not try to train through it. Leaving is a win, not a failure.
- Border collie mix at 14 months needs an outlet or the arousal has nowhere to go. Add 10-15 min/day of nose work or a puzzle feeder, and use the long line in open space at quiet times. Sniffing is calming and lowers baseline arousal — this makes the reactivity work easier, so it is part of the plan, not a nice-to-have.

LOOSE-LEASH DRILLS — 2 x 5 minutes daily, indoors/back garden/driveway only:
1. Reward position: every time he's beside you with a loose leash, mark and feed AT YOUR KNEE. Feed the position you want. High rate of reinforcement, 10-15 treats in five minutes.
2. Stop-and-still: the instant the leash goes tight, stop dead. Do not pull back, do not yank. Wait. The moment there's slack or he glances back, mark and move off again. The lesson is: tight leash = the walk stops, loose leash = the walk continues.
3. Direction reversal: if he forges, turn and walk the other way. Unpredictable direction makes staying near you the winning strategy.

END-OF-WEEK CHECK: can he walk 20 steps on a loose leash in the driveway, and does the U-turn work on a treat lure without him bracing?

subtasks.title: Week 2: add Engage-Disengage Level 1 at your working distance
subtasks.description:
GOAL FOR THE WEEK: change how he FEELS about seeing a dog, before asking him to do anything different. Keep the loose-leash drills running.

ENGAGE-DISENGAGE, LEVEL 1 (the core exercise). Karen Pryor protocol:
1. Park yourself at a distance where he notices dogs but does NOT react — your working distance from week 0. Be quiet and still; let him spot the dog himself. Don't cue him.
2. The precise moment he ENGAGES (looks at the dog) — CLICK.
3. When he turns his head back to you after the click, feed the high-value treat.
4. If he reacts, or doesn't turn back after the click, you are too close. Move further away and reset. Being too close is the only real mistake in this exercise.

Target: 3-5 successful reps in a row at the same distance. A success = he turns back to you immediately after the click. Do not shrink the distance until you have that.

WHERE TO PRACTISE: this needs dogs at a predictable distance, which is why random walks are bad practice ground. Better: sit on a bench 100+ ft from a park entrance or a busy path; park across the street from a pet shop at a busy hour; stand at the far end of a car park near a dog-walking route. You control the distance, so you control whether he succeeds.

DOSE: 3-4 sessions this week, 5-10 minutes each. STOP EARLY. Short and successful beats long and over-threshold. Quit while he's still winning.

BAIL-OUT SIGNALS — end the session the moment you see: excessive lip-licking, yawning, scratching, stiffening, or fixating on a dog for more than 5 seconds. These are stress signals, not stubbornness.

LOOSE-LEASH: keep 2 x 5 min daily, and start moving it to the quiet street rather than the driveway.

END-OF-WEEK CHECK: 5 clean engage-and-return reps at your working distance, and he's eating treats readily with a dog in view.

subtasks.title: Week 3: Engage-Disengage Level 2 + close the distance slightly
subtasks.description:
GOAL FOR THE WEEK: teach him to look away from the dog on his own. Level 2 rewards a behaviour that is physically incompatible with barking and lunging.

ENGAGE-DISENGAGE, LEVEL 2:
1. Let him notice the dog, then WAIT 1-5 seconds. Say nothing. See whether he chooses to look away by himself.
2. The precise moment he DISENGAGES (looks away from the dog) — CLICK, then feed.
3. If he fixates for more than 5 seconds, drop back to Level 1 for a few reps. If he reacts, increase distance.

Only work Level 2 at a distance where Level 1 was already fluent. Before you close distance at all, make sure Level 1 works with dogs approaching from every direction and at different speeds — a dog jogging past at 60 ft is much harder than one standing still at 60 ft.

CLOSING DISTANCE: shrink your working distance in small steps — a few feet, not half the gap. If two reps fail at the new distance, go back to the old one for the rest of the session. Progress here is not linear and one bad session means nothing.

PARALLEL WALKING (optional, if you have a friend with a calm dog): walk both dogs in the same direction, 40-60 ft apart, on parallel paths. No greeting, no head-on approach. Gradually narrow the gap over several sessions. This is far easier for him than a face-to-face pass and builds real-world tolerance fast.

DOSE: 4 sessions, 5-10 minutes each.

LOOSE-LEASH: now practise on real walks, on the quiet routes. Expect it to fall apart when he's aroused — that's normal, drop back to easier ground.

END-OF-WEEK CHECK: he offers a look-away without prompting at least half the time.

subtasks.title: Week 4: combine both skills on a real walk, then reassess
subtasks.description:
GOAL FOR THE WEEK: stitch loose-leash walking and disengagement into one normal evening walk, and decide whether to escalate.

INTEGRATION:
- Walk your normal-ish route, front-clip harness on, high-value treats in hand.
- Default behaviour when a dog appears: he looks, he looks back at you, you feed, you both carry on or U-turn. Practise this as one fluent sequence rather than two separate exercises.
- Keep the U-turn as your escape hatch. Using it is still a win.
- Start varying context deliberately: different streets, dusk vs daylight, dogs behind fences, dogs across a road. Generalisation is a separate skill from the original learning — expect to lose some ground in each new place and rebuild it quickly.
- Begin thinning the treats for LOOSE-LEASH walking only (reward every third or fourth good stretch instead of every one). Do NOT thin the treats for dog-sightings yet — that pairing needs to stay rich for months.

REASSESS AGAINST YOUR WEEK 0 BASELINE. Pull out the notes and answer:
- Has the barking distance shrunk? (Can a dog be closer before he erupts?)
- Is he recovering faster after a reaction?
- Is he checking in with you unprompted when he spots a dog?
- Is the leash tight less of the time?

IF YES, EVEN SLIGHTLY: keep going. Continue weeks 5-8 on the same structure, closing distance gradually. Consider HSSV Top Dogs Level 2 ($300, six weeks, IN PERSON with other reactive dogs) as the natural next step — that's the graduation exercise you can't manufacture yourself.

IF NO MOVEMENT, OR IT'S WORSE: stop self-directing and book a private trainer. Start with Stacy's Wag'N'Train — $190 for a one-hour behaviour consultation, and it's credited free into a package if you continue (Stacy@wagntrain.com). Bring your week 0 baseline notes and this plan; a trainer who can see what you've already tried gets to the point much faster.

ESCALATE IMMEDIATELY, DON'T WAIT FOR WEEK 4, IF: he bites or tries to bite; you can't find any distance at which he'll eat a treat with a dog in sight; or you start dreading walks.

subtasks.title: Email HSSV to ask about the adopter discount on Top Dogs Level 1
subtasks.description:
Email DogTraining@hssv.org. Ask: (1) whether you qualify for the adopter discount on Top Dogs Level 1, and (2) what the discounted price is.

The discount applies if you adopted within the past year from HSSV itself or from ANY weC.A.R.E. Community Coalition adoption centre — so it's worth asking even if you didn't adopt from HSSV directly. They will send you a discount access code.

Include in the email: where and when you adopted, proof of adoption, the dog's animal ID if you have it, and that you want Top Dogs Level 1.

Full price without discount is $300 for the six-week course.

subtasks.title: Enrol in HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 before the Aug 19 cohort fills
subtasks.description:
THE ONE DECISION THAT MATTERS. $300 (possibly less with adopter discount), six weeks, online via Zoom. Next cohort starts Wed Aug 19 2026 at 6:15pm — an evening slot, so it fits.

Register here: https://pro.gofundme.com/event/e826622
Class info: https://www.hssv.org/behavior-management-classes/

Format: first session 90 minutes, then five sessions of 50 minutes.
Eligibility: dogs 8 months+ (yours is 14 months, fine), no bite history on dogs or people.
Covers: threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, emergency exits, real-life coping skills — i.e. exactly the presenting problem.

After this, Top Dogs Level 2 ($300) is the in-person follow-on where you practise around other reactive dogs in a controlled group. That's the real goal; Level 1 is the prerequisite.
